edition: review copy, brain-computer partnership revision of 1 November 2026

demonstrations.title: Why would students rate 3 as a better odd number than 447?
demonstrations.question: The rule for odd numbers gives 3 and 447 the same answer. What did students rate instead, and did they think rating made sense?

symbols_list.meaning: the remainder when the whole number n is divided by two; every odd number leaves 1
mean of students' ratings from 1 (a very good example) to 7 (a very poor one)

demonstrations.provenance: Reported results quoted from the chapter's account of Armstrong, Gleitman and Gleitman (1983): the 31 students' mean ratings of six odd numbers, the 21 students' percentages saying rating by degree makes no sense, and the two Table 6 means for odd number (3 at 1.0, 447 at 1.9). Only those two Table 6 means are given in the chapter.
demonstrations.assumptions: The ratings are means of students' judgments of how well a number fits their idea or image of odd. The study measured behavior; it did not test why 3 came out ahead or what a mind stores, and it compared no storage models.
demonstrations.prediction: The rule gives every odd number the same answer. Before opening the second group, predict whether students who said rating makes no sense still graded 3 and 447 differently.

reveal.text: All 21 students said it makes no sense to rate odd numbers, yet their means still ran from 1.0 for 3 to 1.9 for 447. The grading did not depend on believing the kind was graded.

demonstrations.takeaway: A membership rule asks whether something qualifies; a typicality rating asks how representative it seems. They can give different answers for the same item.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A system that applies an exact test and a system that ranks by typicality answer different questions. Treating a good rating as proof of membership, or a flat rule as proof that no ranking exists, mixes them up.

sides.brain: Students graded an exact kind. The authors suggested a core rule alongside a separate rough identification process; the study did not test why 3 came out ahead, and every result is behavior, not brain activity.
sides.machine: An exact test such as the remainder gives 3 and 447 the same answer. Any graded score a machine reports for them must come from some other computation, such as a summary of cases.

demonstrations.explanation: Both 3 and 447 leave a remainder of 1 when divided by two, so the rule cannot tell them apart. The students still rated 3 as a better example, at 1.6 against 3.7, a gap of 2.1 points. The second group is the surprising part: every one of the 21 said rating odd numbers by degree makes no sense, and still rated 3 at 1.0 and 447 at 1.9.
demonstrations.check: In the chapter's first experiment, how large is the gap in mean rating between 447 and 3, and which of the six odd numbers was rated best after 3?
demonstrations.answer: 447 minus 3 is 3.7 minus 1.6 = 2.1 rating points. After 3 (1.6) the best-rated was 7 at 1.9.
demonstrations.alt: Dot chart of mean ratings for odd numbers beside bars of the percent of students saying rating by degree makes no sense, by kind.
demonstrations.symbols: n mod 2: the remainder when the whole number n is divided by two; every odd number leaves 1; rating: mean of students' ratings from 1 (a very good example) to 7 (a very poor one)
demonstrations.application: A system that applies an exact test and a system that ranks by typicality answer different questions. Treating a good rating as proof of membership, or a flat rule as proof that no ranking exists, mixes them up.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Group of students: experiment 1 · Kind shown on the right: odd number
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: The rule gives 3 and 447 the same answer, remainder 1. Yet experiment 1's students rated 3 at 1.6 and 447 at 3.7, a gap of 2.1 points on a 7-point scale. For odd number, 100 percent of a separate group said grading makes no sense.

demonstrations.title: Should a new case be judged by an average or by every stored case?
demonstrations.question: Kind A has cases at 2, 3 and 4 and kind B at 1 and 7. Where do the two rules disagree about a new case?

symbols_list.meaning: the position of the new case on the line
a stored case of kind K
the exemplar support for kind K: each stored case counts a third as much for each step of distance

demonstrations.source_section: Would a rating make sense for odd numbers? Twenty-one students said no
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's constructed example (not data): cases at 2, 3, 4 and 1, 7, a new case at 0, and a stored case counting a third as much for each step. The sweep over other positions is the companion's own use of the same two rules.
demonstrations.assumptions: One line, two kinds with fixed cases. The prototype rule uses the plain average; the exemplar rule adds closeness over every stored case with a fixed one-third decay. Real studies of people compared no storage models.
demonstrations.prediction: A new case at 0 is far from both averages (3 and 4). Predict which kind each rule picks.

reveal.text: At 0 the average of A (3) is nearer than the average of B (4), so the prototype rule says A. The exemplar rule says B: its case at 1 is one step away and counts about 0.33, against about 0.16 in total from A's three cases.

demonstrations.takeaway: The same stored cases can give two different labels, so graded ratings alone cannot say which rule a mind uses.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: Few-shot machine classifiers that label a new input by its nearest class average use the first rule; a system that compares with every stored case uses the second. Knowing which one is in use predicts where it will disagree with the other.

sides.brain: Whether a mind keeps one average or each case is open. Graded ratings fit a prototype account but do not prove one, and the odd-number studies compared no storage models.
sides.machine: In prototypical networks (Snell and colleagues, 2017) a class's prototype is the average of its embedded cases and a new input goes to the nearest one. The word is borrowed from psychology and the authors do not claim to model human concepts.

demonstrations.explanation: The prototype rule keeps only one number per kind. The exemplar rule keeps every case and lets a nearby stored case count a lot. A new case at 0 sits close to B's single case at 1, so the exemplar rule favors B even though A's average is nearer. Moving the new case along the line shows two stretches where the rules answer differently.
demonstrations.check: For a new case at 5, which kind does the prototype rule pick, and which does the exemplar rule pick?
demonstrations.answer: Distances to the averages are 2 (A at 3) and 1 (B at 4), so the prototype rule says B. The exemplar support is (1/3)^3 + (1/3)^2 + (1/3)^1 = 0.481 for A and (1/3)^4 + (1/3)^2 = 0.123 for B, so the exemplar rule says A.
demonstrations.alt: A number line with kind A and B cases and a new case, beside bands showing where the prototype and exemplar rules answer A or B.
demonstrations.symbols: x: the position of the new case on the line; c: a stored case of kind K; S_K(x): the exemplar support for kind K: each stored case counts a third as much for each step of distance
demonstrations.application: Few-shot machine classifiers that label a new input by its nearest class average use the first rule; a system that compares with every stored case uses the second. Knowing which one is in use predicts where it will disagree with the other.
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: A new case at 0 goes to A by the average and to B by total closeness to stored cases, so they disagree. The same cases can get two labels, so graded ratings alone cannot say which rule a mind uses.

demonstrations.title: How does a feature weight change which stored case is nearest?
demonstrations.question: A new case differs from stored case P mostly in size and from stored case Q mostly in angle. Which is nearer as the weight on size changes?

symbols_list.meaning: the weighted squared distance between cases x and z
a feature; here size and angle
the weight on feature k, nonnegative, all weights add to one
the two cases' values on feature k

demonstrations.source_section: Sixteen semicircles, and weights that followed the task
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's weighted-distance equation. The positions (new case at 2, 2; P at 4, 2; Q at 3, 4 on a four-by-four grid like the 16 semicircles) are constructed by the companion; they are not Nosofsky's stimuli or data.
demonstrations.assumptions: Two features, weights adding to one. The cases are made up. The weights in Nosofsky's study were estimated from choices; attention was never manipulated, so they describe a pattern without showing a cause.
demonstrations.prediction: P is 2 steps off in size only. Q is 1 step off in size and 2 in angle. Predict whether the weight on size must be above or below one half for P to be nearer.

reveal.text: At weights 0.8 and 0.2 a size gap counts four times an equal angle gap, as in the chapter. P then scores 3.2 and Q only 1.6, so Q is nearer. The swap is at a size weight of 4/7, about 0.571.

demonstrations.takeaway: What counts as alike depends on how much each feature is weighted, so the nearest stored case can change when the weights change.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A distance with fixed weights bakes in a view of which features matter. Changing the purpose can change the weights and with them the answer.

sides.brain: In the semicircle study the fitted weights followed the task: where size alone decided the kind, the weight on angle fell to nearly zero. That is a model fitted to choices of two paid observers.
sides.machine: A task weight over features is fixed for a task. Transformer attention, by contrast, is worked out afresh for each input, so the machine parallel is only partial.

demonstrations.explanation: Each feature's gap is squared, scaled by its weight and added. P differs only in size, so its distance is 4 times the size weight. Q differs a little in size and a lot in angle, so its distance shrinks as the angle weight falls. At small size weights P is nearer; once size dominates, Q is.
demonstrations.check: With a size weight of 0.5, what are the squared distances to P and to Q?
demonstrations.alt: A grid with a new case, stored cases P and Q and an equal-distance curve, beside lines of squared distance to P and Q against the size weight.
demonstrations.symbols: d_w^2(x,z): the weighted squared distance between cases x and z; k: a feature; here size and angle; w_k: the weight on feature k, nonnegative, all weights add to one; x_k, z_k: the two cases' values on feature k
demonstrations.application: A distance with fixed weights bakes in a view of which features matter. Changing the purpose can change the weights and with them the answer.
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: With weights 0.5 on size and 0.5 on angle, the squared distances are 2 to P and 2.5 to Q, so P is nearer. Changing what counts can change which stored case is nearest.

demonstrations.title: Can a category win without any single decisive match?
demonstrations.question: Category A has matches of 0.6 and a second one; category B has a single match. How does a category's share come out, and when does the total disagree with the best single match?

symbols_list.meaning: the similarity of the new case to stored case c
a category's total similarity over its stored cases
A's share of the total, when no category is given extra bias

demonstrations.source_section: Sixteen semicircles, and weights that followed the task
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's constructed example: A has partial matches of 0.6 and 0.2, B has one of 0.4, and A's share is about 0.67. The practice question (B rising to 0.8 gives a share of 1/2) is in the book's back matter. Other values are the companion's own variation.
demonstrations.assumptions: Equal response bias for the two categories, as in the chapter. The similarities are chosen by hand and no data stand behind them.
demonstrations.prediction: A has 0.6 and 0.2 and B has 0.4. Predict how large B's single match must be before A's share falls to one half.

reveal.text: B's match of 0.7 is higher than any single match of A (0.6), yet A's total of 0.8 still wins, with a share of 0.533. A category can win through several partial matches even when no single case is decisive.

demonstrations.takeaway: Adding similarities over every stored case can pick a different category from the single best match.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A rule that reads only the single closest case and a rule that sums over all cases behave differently near a boundary. Which one a system uses decides how it treats one strong lookalike against several moderate ones.

sides.brain: The semicircle model fit well, accounting for between about three quarters and nearly all of the pattern in the choices. It is a fitted model of two observers' behavior.
sides.machine: A system that sums similarity over stored cases is computing this rule as a specification; whether a given trained model does so internally is a separate question.

demonstrations.explanation: Each category's support is the sum of the similarities to its stored cases, and dividing by the sum over both gives a share. With two partial matches A reaches 0.8 and B's single 0.4 gives it only a third of the total. Raising B's match to 0.8 ties the totals. At 0.7, B owns the best single match, but A's two matches still add to more.
demonstrations.check: With A's matches 0.6 and 0.2, what share does A hold when B's one match is 0.8?
demonstrations.answer: A's total is 0.8, B's is 0.8, and A's share is 0.8/(0.8 + 0.8) = 1/2.
demonstrations.alt: Stacked bars of summed similarity for categories A and B, beside curves of A's share against the similarity of B's match.
demonstrations.symbols: s(c): the similarity of the new case to stored case c; support(K): a category's total similarity over its stored cases; P(A): A's share of the total, when no category is given extra bias
demonstrations.application: A rule that reads only the single closest case and a rule that sums over all cases behave differently near a boundary. Which one a system uses decides how it treats one strong lookalike against several moderate ones.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Similarity of B's one match: 0.4 · Similarity of A's second match: 0.2
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: A holds 0.8 from its matches and B 0.4, so A's share is 0.667. By total support the winner is A; by the single best match it is A.

demonstrations.title: What should a compact summary keep: shape or color?
demonstrations.question: An object has a shape bit and a color bit. Which of four summaries scores lowest when the target is shape, and what happens if the target or the trade-off weight changes?

symbols_list.meaning: the input, here the object with its shape bit and color bit
the summary; its cost is the bits it keeps about X
the target, the signal the summary must predict (shape or color)
the trade-off weight, zero or more, chosen first

demonstrations.source_section: A toy summary that keeps shape and drops color
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's constructed example (not data): two independent fair bits, four summaries and a weight set by hand to 2. The practice questions (weights 0 and 1) are the same toy at other weights. The paper behind the idea (Tishby, Pereira and Bialek) contains no data and no shape-and-color case.
demonstrations.assumptions: A summary keeps whole properties. Each property is one independent fair bit. The target is named before the summary is chosen, and the weight is set by hand; the paper itself says there is no single right solution for the trade-off.
demonstrations.prediction: At weight 2 and target shape, predict the lowest score and which summary reaches it. Then predict what happens at weight 0.

reveal.text: Keeping shape only scores 1 - 2 = -1, below keeping both (0), color only (1) and nothing (0). No summary can score below -1 at this weight, since shape carries one bit and keeping shape reaches that bound.

demonstrations.takeaway: A summary is good for a purpose, and the purpose is the target: change it and the winner changes.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A compact code that keeps color and drops a faint marking can score well on average and still miss the cases that matter. Someone has to name the purpose before the summary can be judged.

sides.brain: The toy does not explain the odd-number ratings and the bottleneck paper has no brain evidence. It is a way to say what a concept keeps, not a claim about what a mind keeps.
sides.machine: A designer or user has to decide what the system should preserve. In the toy the chosen purpose decides the winner.

demonstrations.explanation: Each summary pays one point per bit it keeps about the object and earns beta points per bit it keeps about the target. With a large enough weight, keeping the target wins. With weight 0 the target earns nothing, so keeping nothing wins. At weight 1 keeping shape and keeping nothing tie, and the rule alone does not choose between them.
demonstrations.check: Target shape, weight 1. Which summaries tie for the lowest score?
demonstrations.answer: Scores are 1 (both), 0 (shape only), 1 (color only) and 0 (nothing), so shape only and nothing tie at 0.
demonstrations.alt: Horizontal bars of the scores of four summaries, beside lines of each summary's score against the trade-off weight.
demonstrations.symbols: X: the input, here the object with its shape bit and color bit; T: the summary; its cost is the bits it keeps about X; Y: the target, the signal the summary must predict (shape or color); beta: the trade-off weight, zero or more, chosen first
demonstrations.application: A compact code that keeps color and drops a faint marking can score well on average and still miss the cases that matter. Someone has to name the purpose before the summary can be judged.
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: With target shape and weight 2, the lowest score is -1, won by keep shape only. Changing the target or the weight changes the winner, because the purpose decides what is worth keeping.

demonstrations.title: Why is the middle level of a name called basic?
demonstrations.question: Students listed attributes for names at three levels. Which step adds the most shared attributes?

symbols_list.meaning: average shared attributes at the superordinate, basic and subordinate levels: 3.5, 9.05 and 11.07

demonstrations.source_section: Names favor a middle level, and color words sat near a best trade-off
demonstrations.provenance: Reported result, quoted from the chapter's account of Rosch and colleagues (1976): 200 students, 90 object names in nine taxonomies. The averages 3.5, 9.05 and 11.07 are the book's averages of the paper's raw tallies over six taxonomies (trees, fish and birds left out), not figures printed in the paper. The ratios computed here are the companion's arithmetic on them.
demonstrations.assumptions: The counts are attributes listed by at least six of 20 students. The study counted attributes; it fit no trade-off to these counts, and reading the middle level as a good trade is the chapter's interpretation, not the paper's.
demonstrations.prediction: The most specific level holds the most shared attributes. Predict what share of the whole rise comes in the first step, from the broad name to the middle name.

reveal.text: The first step adds 5.55 of the whole 7.57, about 0.73, roughly three quarters. The second step adds only 2.02. The biggest jump comes at the middle level.

demonstrations.takeaway: The middle level is basic because the largest gain in shared attributes comes there, even though the most specific level holds the most in total.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A name that buys a lot of shared structure at a small cost is useful for a mind or a system that must label things cheaply. Counting where the gain is largest, not where the total is largest, picks that level.

sides.brain: The students' lists are behavior. The chapter notes a related result on color words in 111 languages scored against a best possible trade-off, but the paper does not show that speakers compute a trade-off.
sides.machine: A system with a bottleneck cost could look for the level where one label buys the most for its cost. That is the chapter's interpretation, not a result of the study.

demonstrations.explanation: Going from the broad name to the middle name adds 5.55 shared attributes. Going on to the most specific name adds only 2.02 more. The specific name still has the highest total, which is why the basic level is chosen by the size of the jump and not by the largest count.
demonstrations.check: What share of the whole rise from 3.5 to 11.07 happens in the first step?
demonstrations.answer: The whole rise is 11.07 - 3.5 = 7.57, the first step is 9.05 - 3.5 = 5.55, and 5.55/7.57 = 0.733.
demonstrations.alt: Bars of average shared attributes at three naming levels beside bars of the attributes added by each step between levels.
demonstrations.symbols: A_super, A_basic, A_sub: average shared attributes at the superordinate, basic and subordinate levels: 3.5, 9.05 and 11.07
demonstrations.application: A name that buys a lot of shared structure at a small cost is useful for a mind or a system that must label things cheaply. Counting where the gain is largest, not where the total is largest, picks that level.
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: At the basic level the average is 9.05 shared attributes. The first step, from 3.5 to 9.05, adds 5.55, which is 0.733 of the whole rise of 7.57. That is why the middle level is called basic.
